content: 1. Aspirin can enhance the pharmacological effects of nitroglycerin when administered together. This interaction may lead to increased vasodilation and hemodynamic effects. Close monitoring is recommended when these drugs are used concomitantly. 2. Aspirin and noni juice both increase serum potassium levels. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but caution and monitoring are advised. 3. Aspirin increases serum potassium levels, while norepinephrine decreases them. The net effect of this interaction is not well understood, so caution and close monitoring are necessary. 4. Aspirin and ofloxacin may interact, potentially increasing the risk of central nervous system stimulation or seizures. This is thought to occur due to displacement of GABA from its receptors in the brain. Close monitoring is advised. 5. Aspirin and olmesartan may increase each other’s toxicity. Aspirin can also reduce the antihypertensive effects of olmesartan through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Both drugs can increase serum potassium levels. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 6. Patients taking omega-3 fatty acids and aspirin should be monitored periodically for an increased risk of bleeding, especially if they are also on anticoagulants or other drugs affecting coagulation. 7. Aspirin and ospemifene may increase each other’s levels due to competition for plasma protein binding. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 8. Aspirin and oxacillin may increase each other’s levels through competition for plasma protein binding or by reducing renal clearance. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 9. Aspirin and oxaprozin both increase anticoagulation and serum potassium levels. Aspirin may also increase oxaprozin levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is advised. 10. Aspirin and panax ginseng both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and monitoring are necessary. 11. Aspirin and parecoxib both increase anticoagulation and serum potassium levels. Aspirin may also increase parecoxib levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 12. Aspirin may increase paromomycin levels by reducing renal clearance. This interaction is more likely to occur in preterm infants. Close monitoring is advised. 13. Aspirin and paroxetine may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to an increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. SSRIs like paroxetine inhibit serotonin uptake by platelets. Close monitoring is necessary. 14. Aspirin and pau d’arco both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 15. Pegaspargase increases the effects of aspirin through pharmacodynamic synergism, raising the risk of bleeding events. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 16. Aspirin increases pemetrexed levels through an unspecified mechanism. Co-administration with NSAIDs should be avoided or alternative drugs used. If NSAIDs are necessary, patients should be closely monitored for toxicity, including myelosuppression, renal toxicity, and gastrointestinal toxicity. 17. Aspirin reduces the effects of penbutolol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Long-term NSAID use may also increase serum potassium levels. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 18. Aspirin and penicillin G aqueous may increase each other’s levels through competition for plasma protein binding or by reducing renal clearance. Caution and monitoring are advised. 19. Aspirin and penicillin VK may increase each other’s levels by reducing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 20. Aspirin and pentazocine may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Chronic use may increase the risk of renal papillary necrosis. Close monitoring is advised. 21. Aspirin and perindopril may increase each other’s toxicity. Co-administration may significantly reduce renal function, and NSAIDs may diminish the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors like perindopril. Therapy modification or alternative drugs are recommended. 22. Aspirin and phenindione both enhance anticoagulation. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 23. Aspirin reduces the effects of phenoxybenzamine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. NSAIDs decrease prostaglandin synthesis. Caution and monitoring are necessary. 24. Aspirin reduces the effects of phentolamine through pharmacodynamic antagonism. NSAIDs decrease prostaglandin synthesis. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 25. Aspirin and phytoestrogens both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and monitoring are advised. 26. Aspirin reduces the effects of pindolol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Long-term NSAID use may also increase serum potassium levels. Caution and monitoring are necessary. 27. Aspirin and piperacillin may increase each other’s effects through receptor binding competition. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 28. Aspirin increases serum potassium levels, while pirbuterol decreases them. The net effect of this interaction is unclear, so caution and close monitoring are advised. 29. Aspirin and piroxicam both enhance anticoagulation and increase serum potassium levels. Aspirin may also increase piroxicam levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 30. Aspirin and potassium acid phosphate both increase serum potassium levels. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 31. Aspirin and potassium chloride both increase serum potassium levels. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary. 32. Aspirin and potassium citrate both increase serum potassium levels. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 33. Aspirin and potassium iodide both increase serum potassium levels. Caution and monitoring are advised. 34. Aspirin and prasugrel may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Patients with cardiovascular disease often require low-dose aspirin and anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents, necessitating close monitoring. 35. Aspirin reduces the effects of prazosin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. NSAIDs decrease prostaglandin synthesis. Caution and monitoring are necessary. 36. Aspirin and prednisolone may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Prednisolone may also reduce aspirin levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 37. Aspirin and prednisone may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Prednisone may also reduce aspirin levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but caution and monitoring are advised. 38. Aspirin reduces the effects of probenecid by competing for renal tubular clearance. This reduces the uricosuric action of probenecid. Co-administration should be avoided or alternative drugs used. 39. Aspirin reduces the effects of propranolol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Long-term NSAID use may also increase serum potassium levels. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 40. Aspirin and protamine both enhance anticoagulation. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. 41. Aspirin and quinapril may increase each other’s toxicity. Co-administration may significantly reduce renal function, and NSAIDs may diminish the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors like quinapril. Therapy modification or alternative drugs are recommended. 42. Aspirin and ramipril may increase each other’s toxicity. Co-administration may significantly reduce renal function, and NSAIDs may diminish the antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors like ramipril. Therapy modification or alternative drugs are recommended. 43. Aspirin and reishi both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and monitoring are necessary. 44. Aspirin and reteplase may increase each other’s toxicity through enhanced anticoagulation. Patients with cardiovascular disease often require low-dose aspirin and anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents, necessitating close monitoring. 45. Aspirin and rivaroxaban may increase each other’s toxicity through enhanced anticoagulation. Both drugs have the potential to cause bleeding. Patients with cardiovascular disease often require low-dose aspirin and anticoagulants, necessitating close monitoring. Prompt evaluation of any signs of blood loss is recommended. 46. Rivastigmine increases the toxicity of aspirin through pharmacodynamic synergism. Patients should be monitored for symptoms of active or occult gastrointestinal bleeding. 47. Rose hips may increase aspirin levels by decreasing renal clearance, while aspirin may reduce rose hips levels by increasing renal clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is advised. 48. Aspirin and sacubitril/valsartan may increase each other’s toxicity. Aspirin reduces the effects of sacubitril/valsartan through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Both drugs can increase serum potassium levels. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended. 49. Aspirin and salicylates (non-ASA) both enhance anticoagulation and increase serum potassium levels. Aspirin may also increase salicylate levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is advised. 50. Aspirin increases serum potassium levels, while salmeterol decreases them. The net effect of this interaction is unclear, so caution and close monitoring are necessary. 51. Aspirin and salsalate both enhance anticoagulation and increase serum potassium levels. Aspirin may also increase salsalate levels by competing for renal tubular clearance. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but close monitoring is recommended. 52. Saw palmetto increases the toxicity of aspirin through an unspecified mechanism. This may increase the risk of bleeding. Caution and monitoring are advised. 53. Aspirin and selumetinib both enhance anticoagulation. Patients taking a vitamin K antagonist or an antiplatelet agent with selumetinib may have an increased risk of bleeding. Monitoring for bleeding and INR or PT is recommended. 54. Aspirin and sertraline may increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to an increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. SSRIs like sertraline inhibit serotonin uptake by platelets. Close monitoring is necessary. 55. Aspirin and Siberian ginseng both enhance anticoagulation. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 56. Aspirin reduces the effects of silodosin through pharmacodynamic antagonism. NSAIDs decrease prostaglandin synthesis. Caution and monitoring are necessary. 57. Sodium bicarbonate may alter salicylate levels by increasing renal tubular reabsorption at moderate doses or increasing renal excretion at high doses. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but caution and monitoring are advised. 58. Sodium citrate/citric acid may alter salicylate levels by increasing renal tubular reabsorption at moderate doses or increasing renal excretion at high doses. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 59. Aspirin and sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid may increase each other’s toxicity. Co-administration may be associated with fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Caution and monitoring are advised. 60. Magnesium sulfate/potassium chloride may increase the toxicity of aspirin. Co-administration with medications causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Caution and monitoring are necessary. 61. Sodium sulfate/potassium sulfate/magnesium sulfate may increase the toxicity of aspirin. Co-administration with medications causing fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Caution and monitoring are advised. 62. Aspirin reduces the effects of sotalol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Long-term NSAID use may also increase serum potassium levels. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 63. Aspirin and sparsentan both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Co-administration of NSAIDs, including selective COX-2 inhibitors, may result in increased risk. Caution and monitoring are advised.
